questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to a medium-size city, outside of the EU, and preferably somewhere they spoke English, French or Spanish, giving me an opportunity to practice my language skills.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: McGill sends out a lot of information about orientation events for first-year students as well as exchange students, so it was easy to sign-up for events and know when and where things were happening! They give you a virtual brochure, highlighting the most important information and describing the different neighbourhoods which was quite useful.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was some initial orientation events before classes started, which was nice to get an overview of the semester, key academic dates, requirements etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: We were four students looking for a shared apartment and were quite lucky in terms of finding housing last minute – but this is definitely not what I would recommend. As soon as you get accepted, start looking for places! There are also many other students from KU going to McGill, so the Facebook group with everybody is a good place to start if you're looking for roommates. We found our apartment through Facebook as well, but be aware since there a many stories of scams.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is the cheapest option, but can be a little tricky if you're looking last minute. We lived just across campus, but there are many other nice neighbourhoods near McGill that are also great options, especially Plateau!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I think registration opened in early June (but I'm not 100% sure), but I only registered for courses in mid/end July. 
McGill has a "Drag and Drop" period in the first two weeks after classes start, which means in this period a lot of students drop some classes and sign up for others – so don't worry if you are not able to register for all the classes you want from the beginning, chances are you will probably get in during this period. For the classes with waitlists, definitely sign up for the waitlist! You can always drop it in the first two weeks.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I don't remember exactly what help (if any) I used, but I know that on McGill's website they have a bunch of guides for incoming students, which are quite useful!

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted after the "Drag and Drop" period!

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Look through the course catalogue and get a good idea of which courses you want to take! Note that some are only offered during winter, so if you are going abroad in the fall semester disregard these. 
Sign up as early as you can, but if you can't register for some of the courses you want, don't worry – chances are you'll probably get it once classes start and people decide to switch. 
Importantly, if you are in doubt which courses you want to take, attend as many as you want/can during the first two weeks, to get a better idea and then decide afterwards!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The courses for undergraduate students (us) go from level 100 to 500. The 100 courses are often very introductory, and the 500 courses are supposed to be the most difficult. I took one 200-level course, two 300-level and one 400-level course. 
In the end it was the 200 level course that required the most of my attention, since it had weekly quizzes and assignments, whereas the 400 level course was more chill and similar to the courses we have at KU, where the student can decide how to structure time and workload.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I think the teaching style was similar to the one at UCPH. My 400-level course was in a small classroom setting, whereas the other three courses were in big auditoriums with 70+ students. I would say the material and level of the courses are also similar to the level at UCPH, but note that the semester at McGill is shorter than at UCPH, so you need to learn and study the material in a shorter amount of time – hence, it can feel like more work than we are used to from home.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
COMP 204 – Computer Programming for Life Sciences
PHGY 314 - Integrative Neuroscience
ANAT 321 – Circuitry of the Human Brain
PHGY 488 – Stem Cell Biology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I cannot recommend the course ANAT 321 – Circuitry of the Human Brain enough! It was the best course I have had in my education thus far. The instructor is absolutely amazing and every lecture feels like a Ted Talk! Even if you don't find neuroscience interesting, I would still recommend taking this course. It was also the course with the lowest workload and the best/easiest exams! 
COMP204 had the highest workload but it gives a good basis idea of programming, especially if you have zero coding experience (like me). 
PHGY 314 had a lot of similar content to ANAT 321 but on a higher and more detailed level – I would recommend it if you find neuroscience interesting. 
PHGY 488 was an ok course, the material is somewhat similar to what we have learned in Molecular Biology. There is no midterm, which was nice.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I don't think there we any unexpected costs – we did a lot of travelling to nearby cities, which obviously makes the journey more expensive than if you stay in Montreal the entire semester. I did not include the costs for travels etc. in the information above.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were quite expensive, but I believe that was mostly because the only supermarket near our apartment was quite fancy – I imagine the prices were similar to buying groceries in Meny in Copenhagen. Other than that, the majority of things were cheaper than in Copenhagen. A good cup of coffee cost around 25 DKK for reference.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I did a yoga class and a barre class through McGill, which is cheaper than doing them in a studio, and a good option. They sell out fast so buy them early on! There are endless options of sports you can do through McGill, where you pay for the entire semester. I paid 75 CAD total for the entire term, but the price depends on which class you choose. 
There are also a huge amount of clubs for many different interests that you can engage in at McGill, like knitting club, wine club, salsa club etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Whatever your interests, find a club that matches them! It is a great way to meet new people. 
I liked my yoga and pilates class, so would definitely recommend them if it interests you:)

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go on trips! We went to Toronto, New York, Québec and Banff throughout the semester, which are all great destinations! 
Pro tip: You don't need more than a day to see Québec, and I'd recommend going in December to see the Christmas market.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I think it was pretty easy, Canadians are very open and welcoming! Everyone in the city speak both French and English, so it is easy to get by even if you don't speak French:)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs or sports!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I didn't find any cultural differences challenging!

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness and openness of the Canadians! It makes it very easy to feel included and make friends.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Since we don't get Erasmus for studying in Canada, I would recommend applying for scholarships and/or save money before going, so you don't need to worry too much about costs etc while you're abroad:) 
Make use of the holidays, or the fact that most lectures are recorded, to go on trips! 
Explore the city early on in the semester! We ended up saving many touristy things for last, thinking we would have plenty of time – we did not. Once midterms begin, time goes really fast and you will have more work to do.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: One of the things that will probably come up as an option in the beginning is FROSH. It is a few days of many introductory events and activities before classes start, but it is primarily for the students starting their first semester at McGill. We thought there might be other exchange students, but it was mostly 17 and 18-year olds students. It is quite expensive to participate, so I don't think it is worth the time and price. Instead, I would check out the events for exchange students, which are very fun and a good way to get to know the city.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to live in a new city;)

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I don't think there was any!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go on exchange!!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
